title: Dobar tek!
theme: Restaurant debate over klepe and japrak
reviewerNotes: This full draft is ready for human review before publication.
storyBeat: Ana and Emir debate klepe versus japrak at a Sarajevo restaurant.

vocabulary: Order klepe or japrak from a restaurant menu.
Use waiter, bill, and meal-wish words at the table.
Describe food as ukusan or ukusna.
grammar: Use hoću, hoćeš, and hoćemo to say what you want.
Order with molim and ask for račun politely.
Say Dobar tek when the food arrives.
culture: Compare klepe and japrak as beloved Bosnian dishes.
Keep Visoko on the wider food map with a postcard.
Notice hospitality as part of everyday recovery.

grammar.title: Hoću, hoćeš, hoćemo
grammar.explanation: Hoću means I want, hoćeš asks or states what you want, and hoćemo covers we want. Keep all three in the present for now. You can learn past and future forms later.

grammar.title: Ordering with molim and račun
grammar.explanation: Place the food word first, then molim. When you finish, say Račun, molim for the bill. A little politeness keeps any restaurant scene smooth.

grammar.title: Dobar tek at the table
grammar.explanation: Dobar tek wishes someone an enjoyable meal. Say it when the food arrives, then answer with Hvala. The phrase works among friends and with restaurant staff alike.

culture.title: Klepe, japrak, and a full table
culture.body: Sarajevo restaurants still see friendly arguments over favorite dishes when friends share a table. Klepe are soft dumplings often served with sauce and a garlic yogurt topping. Japrak wraps rice and meat in vine leaves and arrives as neat rolls that invite a slow bite. Ana and Emir open a jelovnik and turn their debate into practice with hoću and hoćeš. A Visoko postcard on the table reminds them that Bosnian food stories reach well beyond one city street. Saying Dobar tek marks the meal as a shared moment before anyone reaches for the bill.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson A. Wanting food with htjeti
lessonBlocks.body: Learn restoran, jelovnik, konobar, klepe, and japrak first so the room has clear names. Then practice Hoću, Hoćeš li, and Hoćemo as ready lines for saying what you want. Ana wants klepe, Emir wants japrak, and their friendly disagreement carries the lesson. Point at the menu and say the food word with molim instead of building a long sentence. Stay in the present, and your order is ready for a real waiter tonight. Practice each dish name a couple of times, then switch roles so both of you can ask and answer with hoćeš. Keep these lines short and ready to reuse at any table.
tips: Say Hoću plus the dish as one ready line.
Use Hoćeš li for a friendly question.
Keep htjeti in the present only.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson B. From order to račun
lessonBlocks.body: Build the full table flow from greeting to goodbye, all in short present-tense lines. Greet, order with hoću, wish Dobar tek, ask for još if you need more bread, then call for račun. Say Hvala after every helpful move from the konobar so your politeness stays audible. Amira may show up with an opinion, and Mrvica watches for crumbs under the table as always. The Visoko postcard keeps the meal tied to a wider map of Bosnian kitchens beyond Sarajevo. Practice the debate until both dishes feel easy to say and easy to defend with a smile. Finish by asking for the bill in a calm, polite voice.
tips: Add molim to every order and to Račun, molim.
Name both dishes so the debate stays balanced.

funFacts.title: Klepe come with sauce and garlic
funFacts.body: Klepe are boiled dumplings that often arrive with a savory sauce. Many diners add a garlic yogurt topping at the table. The dish feels homey even in a busy restaurant. Ana's order makes this soft dumpling worth learning by heart.

funFacts.title: Japrak wraps the vine leaf
funFacts.body: Japrak uses vine leaves wrapped around a rice and meat filling. The rolls cook slowly and taste bright with lemon or sauce. Emir defends japrak as the better choice. The debate keeps both food names in active use.

funFacts.title: Visoko sits on the food map
funFacts.body: A postcard from Visoko reminds diners that Bosnian kitchens are not only a Sarajevo story. Towns across the country share related stuffed and dough dishes, each with its own local twist. The card widens the meal without leaving the table, and geography becomes part of the restaurant chat.

civicContext.title: Neighbor passports split mobility at the same table
civicContext.body: Shared food does not mean equal travel papers. Many Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Serbs can hold Croatian or Serbian citizenship while still living in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Those neighbor-state passports can open European Union travel and paperwork routes that many Bosniak neighbors cannot match through residence alone. A restaurant debate over klepe and japrak happens in a country where the document in your pocket can depend on ethnic background as much as the street where you sleep.
